title: Outbox Pattern
description: Learn the outbox pattern to reliably publish events from microservices.

data.text: The outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem: how to update a database and publish an event atomically. Amazon, Netflix, and LinkedIn all use the outbox pattern to ensure events are never lost, even when services crash after updating the database.

A naive approach updates the database and publishes an event in the same transaction. But if the service crashes after the database commit but before the event is published, the event is lost. The outbox pattern ensures atomicity by storing the event in the same database transaction.

data.title: Outbox Pattern Steps
items: Service updates its database in a transaction
In the same transaction, service inserts the event into an outbox table
A separate process polls the outbox table for unpublished events
The process publishes events to the message broker
After successful publish, the event is marked as published or deleted

data.title: Change Data Capture Alternative
data.text: Instead of polling, you can use CDC (Debezium) to stream outbox table changes to Kafka. This eliminates the polling process and provides near-real-time event publishing.

data.title: Example: Outbox Table Implementation
data.code: Insert an event into the outbox table in the same transaction as the business data.

-- Transaction in Order Service
BEGIN;

-- Update business data
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total, status)
VALUES ('ord-789', 'cust-456', 149.99, 'created');

-- Insert event into outbox (same transaction!)
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, created_at)
VALUES (
  'evt-abc123',
  'Order',
  'ord-789',
  'OrderCreated',
  '{"orderId":"ord-789","total":149.99}',
  NOW()
);

COMMIT;

-- Outbox processor picks up the event and publishes to Kafka

data.caption: Outbox pattern flow
data.definition:
graph LR
    S[Service] -->|1. Transaction| DB[(Database)]
    DB -->|Business data| BD[Business Tables]
    DB -->|Event| OB[Outbox Table]
    P[Outbox Processor] -->|2. Poll| OB
    P -->|3. Publish| M[Message Broker]
    M -->|4. Deliver| C[Consumers]

items.question: How often should I poll the outbox table?
items.answer: Every 1-5 seconds for low-latency requirements. For less critical events, polling every minute reduces database load.

items.question: What if the outbox processor fails?
items.answer: Events remain in the outbox table. When the processor recovers, it publishes all unpublished events. Ensure the processor is idempotent.

items.question: Should I delete outbox events after publishing?
items.answer: Yes, or mark them as published. Keeping them for a few days helps with debugging and replay. Use TTL to auto-clean old events.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Outbox pattern ensures atomic database updates and event publishing
Store events in the same transaction as business data
Use polling or CDC to publish events
data.takeaway: The outbox pattern is essential for reliable event publishing; always use it instead of dual-writes.
